description: We are a multidisciplinary team of students driven by scientific curiosity and critical thinking. We approach challenges through research, evidence-based reasoning, and collaborative problem-solving. For this challenge, we aim to examine the complexities of astronaut health monitoring, identify gaps in existing approaches, and develop a practical, innovative solution. We value diverse perspectives, adaptability, and turning complex ideas into meaningful outcomes.
summary: Baseline is an offline-capable web app that helps astronauts and crew medical officers track their health on long space missions. Each day the crew logs a few simple readings: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, mood, exercise, blood sugar, skin condition and a weekly near-vision test. Baseline compares every reading with that person's own normal baseline, not an Earth average, because fluid shifts, bone loss and muscle loss in space can make Earth values misleading. It shows eight body systems as Normal (green), Watch (yellow) or Act now (red). For each reading it explains how to measure it, why it matters, and what to do when values look abnormal, and it reminds the crew to take their measurements. It adapts to a spacecraft, a space station or a lunar base. The content is built on NASA's Human Research Program hazards and the ISS Spaceflight Standard Measures. It matters because a message to Mars takes about 20 minutes each way, so crews need clear guidance on board. The same idea could inspire health tools for remote communities on Earth.
details:
1.2 What exactly does it do?

Baseline is not a doctor and does not diagnose. It is a decision-support tool that helps an astronaut understand their own body and decide what to do next without needing medical training.

The user can:

  • Set a personal baseline. Each astronaut records their own normal before the flight or in the first week. The app never assumes one "normal" number for everyone.
  • Log daily readings. The astronaut types a number with its unit. Mood and skin use rows of buttons instead. Logging again on the same day replaces the earlier value.
  • See status at a glance. A summary strip shows a readiness score from 0 to 100, the count of Normal, Watch and Act now indicators, and a chip for each indicator that needs attention.
  • Explore a clickable body map. Eight pills (Heart, Lungs, Brain & sleep, Eyes, Bones & muscle, Metabolism, Skin, Immune) sit on either side of a human figure. A system on Watch or Act now gets a pulsing ring.
  • Read a detail panel for each system with the current value, the change from baseline, a 30-day chart, a log box and three guide blocks: How to measure, Why it matters and What to do.
  • Follow a Mission Clock that reminds the crew to take their measurements.
  • Watch for radiation events with the Radiation Watch card and a storm shelter checklist.
  • Stay motivated with Crew Vitality (points, streak, crew exercise goal, badges).
  • Report to the ground with an offline Ground Link report for the flight surgeon.
  • Switch environment between Spacecraft, Space station and Lunar base.

1.3 Benefits

  • Catches slow drift early (fluid shift effects, bone and muscle loss, poor sleep, falling mood).
  • Personal baselines avoid misleading Earth averages.
  • Works offline, which matters when messages to Mars take about 20 minutes each way.
  • Needs no medical training: every reading comes with steps to measure, an explanation and an action.
  • Reduces false alarms through 3-reading averages.
  • Supports mental health with calm wording, escalation to the flight psychologist and a shared crew goal.
  • Accessible: colour plus label plus icon, keyboard use, screen reader announcements, reduced-motion support and large tap targets for gloved hands.
  • Gives the flight surgeon a clear, structured report.

1.4 What do we hope to achieve? What is the intended impact?

We want to give astronauts a simple way to understand their own health during Moon and Mars missions, and to show that a personal-baseline approach can work when help is far away. The intended impact is better crew autonomy, earlier reporting and safer decisions when ground contact is delayed.

We also hope it inspires health self-monitoring tools for remote communities and places with limited access to health services, where the same ideas of personal baselines, clear guidance, offline use and simple reports to a distant clinician also apply.

1.5 What factors did our team consider?

  • Distance and delay: offline use and clear on-board guidance.
  • Personal baselines: fluid shifts and bone and muscle loss make Earth averages misleading, and every astronaut is different.
  • False alarms: averaging for sleep, mood and exercise.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind users, gloved hands, keyboard use, screen readers and reduced motion.
  • Tone: calm and supportive wording, especially for mental health.
  • Honesty: simulated data, illustrative limits, no diagnosis and no real transmission.
  • Environment differences: spacecraft, station and lunar base each have different risks (limited equipment, 90-minute sunrises, lunar dust).

1.6 Tools, languages, hardware and software

  1. HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+)
  2. Figma (UI/UX design, wireframing, prototyping, and design tokens for light and dark themes)
  3. Inline SVG for the interactive body map and the 30-day charts
  4. CSS Grid and Flexbox for a responsive layout (900 px breakpoint)
  5. prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme media features for accessibility and theming
  6. Rule-based status engine (personal baselines, Watch and Act now thresholds, 3-reading moving averages)
  7. In-memory data storage, with optional browser localStorage for the demo
  8. Large touch targets designed for users wearing gloves
  9. Development laptops/PCs and test devices (mobile and desktop)
  10. Modern web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) for testing

1.7 AI tools disclosure

-Claude (Anthropic):

Purpose: To assist in drafting and refining project documentation, to propose the structure of the status logic, and to help write the innovation description.

Human oversight: All concepts, design decisions, thresholds, and health-related content were reviewed and approved by the team. All thresholds are illustrative and do not constitute medical advice.

Not used for: Collecting real patient data. The application uses simulated data only.

1.8 Main game content: the main idea

Every reading is compared with your own normal. The crew plays the astronaut and medical officer: they set their baseline, keep the readiness score high, respond to Watch and Act now alerts, and handle events like a solar particle storm. Gamification keeps the habit going. First daily logs give 10 points, a new level comes every 100 points, streaks track full days of checks, and badges reward good habits. The crew exercise goal of 28 sessions per week gives the team a shared goal against isolation.

Part 2. How the Project Works

2.1 The three statuses (green, yellow, red) and the logic behind them

All eight systems use the same logic, so it is built once and reused.

  1. Personal baseline. Each of the 11 indicators has a baseline, which is the astronaut's own normal, set before the flight or in the first week.
  2. Two limits. Each indicator has a Watch limit and an Act now limit, measured as the change from the person's own baseline (a percent, or a number of points or steps). A direction decides which side counts: both (too high or too low), down only or up only.
  3. Three status levels. Colour is never used alone. Each level has a label and an icon too.
  4. Averaging. Sleep, mood and exercise are judged on the average of the last 3 readings, so one bad night does not turn the screen red. All other indicators use the latest reading.
  5. System status. A system's status is its worst indicator. Brain and sleep is red if either sleep or mood is red.
  6. Readiness score. Start at 100, subtract 5 for each indicator on Watch and 15 for each on Act now, with a minimum of 0. A score of 85 or more is green, 65 to 84 is yellow, and below 65 is red.
  7. Status function. Take the value (the average if the indicator smooths), work out the change from the baseline in the direction that counts, and compare it with the limits. At least the Act now limit gives status 2, at least the Watch limit gives status 1, otherwise 0.
  8. Instant update. After logging, the chart, system status, summary and score all update at once.
  9. Chart. The x axis shows the last 30 mission days. The green band is the normal range, the dashed line is the baseline, each dot is coloured by its status, and a ring marks the latest reading. Averaged indicators also get a moving-average line.

Data model. Small lists drive everything: an indicator record (id, system, name, unit, warn, crit, limit type, direction, smoothingWindow, decimals, min, max), a personal baseline record per astronaut (indicator, baseline value, date set) and a reading record (indicator, day, value). Green (Normal): the reading is inside the astronaut's own range. Nothing to do except keep logging.

Yellow (Watch): the reading is drifting from the astronaut's own baseline. The app shows calm self-management steps.

Red (Act now): the reading has moved far from the baseline. The app shows emergency steps and tells the user to contact the flight surgeon.

2.4 What the crew should do if an indicator is Watch or Act now

Each system has two short videos: a yellow "Be careful" video and a red "Act now" video. Each video also shows how to take the measurement, why it matters and how the advice changes in a spacecraft, space station or lunar base.

System

Watch (yellow)

Act now (red)

Heart

Rest 10 minutes, remeasure, hydrate, check sleep and food

Stop work, secure yourself, check for chest pain, dizziness or breathlessness, tell a crewmate, call the flight surgeon with the trend

Lungs

Re-check after 5 minutes, read cabin O2 and CO2, move to a better ventilated module

Alert the crew, check cabin air alarms, use backup oxygen, call the flight surgeon

Brain, sleep and mood

Fix sleep schedule for 3 nights, dim lights, talk to a crewmate, call home

Tell the commander, ask for a schedule change, contact the flight psychologist ("You do not have to handle this alone")

Eyes

Retest in the same light, rest eyes, report at next call

Tell the flight surgeon, share eye images, avoid close-vision tasks, note flashes or headaches

Bones and muscle

Do a full session, exercise with a crewmate, report broken equipment

Tell commander and ground, ask for a modified plan, avoid skipping days

Metabolism

Retest after a meal or in 2 hours, review food and exercise

Sit down and recheck, tell a crewmate if shaky or confused, call the flight surgeon

Skin

Wash gently, use approved cream, photograph daily

Stop new products or liners, send the photo to the flight surgeon, report fever, pus or fast spreading

Immune and radiation

Rest, fluids, avoid shared food, wipe surfaces; for radiation, spend more time in the best shielded area

Isolate and mask for fever; for radiation, go to the storm shelter now, stay until clear, report exposure

When a system has no specific tip, a general note is shown. Spacecraft: help is far away and messages are slow, so decide with the crew first, then send a clear summary to the ground. Space station: contact with ground is easy, so when unsure, ask the flight surgeon. Lunar base: contact with Earth is almost real time, so use the live link for anything that looks off.

2.6 The other panels

  • Summary strip: readiness score, counts of Normal, Watch and Act now, and chips for each non-normal indicator.
  • Mission Clock: a reminder system for taking measurements (07:30 morning vitals, 08:00 sleep and mood check-in, 18:00 exercise session, weekly near-vision test, skin check every 3 days), with Done or Log states and automatic jumping to the next unfinished reading.
  • Radiation Watch: a dose bar coloured by status, a solar particle event simulation (240% of plan), and a red banner with a checklist (move to the storm shelter, note the time you entered, read and log your dosimeter, tell the crew and ground, and after the all-clear log nausea, tiredness or skin redness), then "Clear alert".
  • Crew Vitality: 10 points for the first log of each indicator each day. Level = points divided by 100, rounded down, plus 1. Streak = days with all checks done. Crew exercise goal = team sessions against 28 per week. Badges: Sleep protected, Strong week, All checks done.
  • Ground Link: a text box for an optional crew note. The report lists mission day, environment and readiness score, then an URGENT line for every indicator on Act now, then one line per indicator (value, unit, baseline, status and change since 7 days ago), then the crew note. The Send button turns red and reads "Send urgent report" when anything is on Act now. Buttons are Send, Copy and a link-loss simulation toggle. With the link down, Send queues the report and sends it when the link returns. The prototype does not transmit anything, and the interface says so.

Disclaimer shown in the app: the demo uses simulated data. The limits are illustrative placeholders, not medical advice, and flight surgeons set the real ones. Baseline helps the crew decide. It does not diagnose.

3.2 NASA data used

  • NASA Human Research Program, five hazards of spaceflight: https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/human-research-program/
  • NASA ISS Spaceflight Standard Measures (behavioral health, cardiovascular, immunology, bone, muscle, eyes and more)
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): https://osdr.nasa.gov/bio/, used for inspiration and to test our ideas against real spaceflight biology data
  • NASA OSDR and Inspiration4 data
  • NASA: experiments on long space journeys

3.3 Space Agency Partner data and other resources

  • Canadian Space Agency: Bio-Monitor and Bio-Analyzer (wearable heart and blood pressure monitoring on the ISS)
  • Spaceflight dermatology with NASA OSDR data
  • Ini make apa
  • AI assistance, as disclosed in section 1.7

3.4 How we integrated NASA data into our story

  1. NASA Human Research Program: we started with the five hazards (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, hostile closed environments) and mapped each one to the body systems it reaches.
  2. ISS Spaceflight Standard Measures: we chose indicators that are actually measured on crews (behavioral health, cardiovascular, immunology, bone, muscle, eyes), so the app tracks realistic readings.
  3. NASA OSDR: we explored the repository for real spaceflight biology data as inspiration and a reality check. It supported the skin system (skin problems are among the most common in-flight issues, including the ISS rash that worsened after a spacewalk) and the metabolism system (spaceflight changes insulin-linked gene activity). Inspiration4 data added to our understanding of how short missions affect the body.
  4. CSA Bio-Monitor and Bio-Analyzer: these supported using wearable heart rate and blood pressure trends.
  5. In the story: the crew becomes the player. Setting a baseline, daily logging, hazards, the solar particle event, the 20-minute Mars delay and the offline Ground Link report shape the readiness score and the decisions the crew must make.
